name: Copper peptide scalp serum
lead: A copper peptide scalp serum is a topical cosmetic product containing GHK-Cu (copper tripeptide-1), a complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine and copper(II), applied to the scalp with the aim of supporting hair growth or thickness.[1]

GHK-Cu occurs naturally in human plasma, saliva and urine, and was isolated from plasma by Loren Pickart in 1973.[1] It is widely used in cosmetics for anti-aging and hair-loss-prevention claims, where it is listed as copper tripeptide-1.[1] Most of the wound-healing evidence cited for GHK-Cu comes from cell cultures and animal studies, and the facial-skin studies that exist are described as small and short.[1]
No clinical studies of scalp copper peptide serums for hair loss were identified for this article.

paras: GHK-Cu is a naturally occurring tripeptide bound to copper. It is proposed to modulate wound healing, attract immune cells, act as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, and stimulate collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis in skin fibroblasts and blood vessel growth.[1] Scalp serums apply the same ingredient to the scalp, often alongside other topical hair products.
Pickart isolated the copper-binding peptide from human plasma albumin in 1973, and in 1977 the growth-modulating peptide was identified as glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine.[1]

No studies found. Related work on GHK-Cu consists largely of cell-culture and animal experiments and a few small, short controlled studies on facial skin; the same source notes that GHK-Cu also increases matrix metalloproteinases, which break down dermal proteins, and that more research is needed.[1]

Copper peptide serums are discussed in hair-loss communities as an add-on to minoxidil or finasteride routines. The mechanism proposed by proponents follows the general GHK-Cu claims above (follicle support, anti-inflammatory action).

timeline.event: Pickart isolates the copper-binding peptide from human plasma.[1]
The peptide is identified as glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine.[1]

card.summary: GHK-Cu peptide serum for the scalp: popular in hair stacks, with no published scalp trials behind it.
card.note: Skin evidence is small and short; no scalp hair trials found.

quick.overview:
Copper peptide scalp serums put GHK-Cu, a small copper-binding peptide found naturally in the body, on the scalp. They are marketed for hair thickness and loss prevention.

Most GHK-Cu research is in cell and animal studies, with a few small facial-skin studies. No scalp hair-loss trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Proposed actions include supporting wound healing, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, and stimulating collagen and blood vessel growth; none of these have been shown for hair in published human trials.
quick.risks: Sold as a cosmetic ingredient. The source notes GHK-Cu also raises matrix metalloproteinases and advises caution; scalp-specific safety data are not available.
